newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end higher, led by PGM problems.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end higher, led by PGM problems.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended higher Thursday, led by gains in platinum prices, amid ongoing talk of delivery problems in the physical market, due to a five month suspension of exports by Russia, the world's largest supplier of platinum group metals (PGMs).

"White metals were the star of the show, but even silver benefitted from the strength of the PGMs and gold looks again to be finding support around $340 an ounce," Chase Manhattan managing director for global commodities, Dinsa Mehta said.

NYMEX July platinum closed bid limit up and settled up $25.00 at a new contract high at $436.60 an ounce, while in the physical market spot platinum was quoted around $446.00 an ounce, after being fixed in London earlier Thursday at $440.00, the highest fixing since September 15, 1995.

"The fundamentals in PGMs look strong, the technicals looks strong, the funds are still buying platinum and few people want to sell it, so platinum closed bid limit up, but palladium trade was mostly in the spreads with the June contract expiring," Pioneer Futures analyst Scott Meyers said.
NYMEX June palladium ended down $2.65 an ounce at $200.15 midday, after some liquidation by a trade house, but not before seeing a new contract high at $214.00 an ounce early.
Deliveries of the NYMEX June palladium contract, due to expire on June 25, were proceeding normally, exchange officials said, though trade houses reported difficulties.

But the real problem lay in the physical market where some bullion banks reported difficulties with deliveries on spot contracts Wednesday and warned of multi-million dollar losses on short positions by some trade houses.

NYMEX warehouse stocks of palladium fell 2,600 ounces to 52,700 ounces Thursday, but open interest in NYMEX June palladium fell 399 lots (39,900 ounces) to 362 contracts (36,200 ounces), removing the threat of a delivery squeeze.
September palladium closed up 35 cents at $173.15.
In the spot market, palladium where quoted was notionally around $213.15, compared to the London Thursday fix at $235.00 an ounce, the highest since fixings began in 1989.
On Wednesday spot palladium reached a 17 year high at $230.00, with one month lease rates jumping to over 150 percent and overnight lease rates over 200 percent.

The shortage of metal forced dealers to stop quoting forward prices and lease rates for PGMs Thursday, and led to a meeting of the ten members London Platinum and Palladium Market Association, held at Standard Bank, in conjunction with a conference call with Zurich dealers.
"The members confirmed that there were no defaults in the market," Association chairman Trevor Pitts said later.

Members agreed forward rates would be done on a "quote suggestion" basis for the time being, which traders said meant quotes would be only indicative and not obligatory, while clients could leave limit-orders for brokers to work.
"There may not have been any technical defaults, but there are certainly difficulties with deliveries," one U.S. refining source said.
"Members agreed to try to offer clients an orderly market in platinum and palladium but the key issue really depends on when the Russians begin exporting again," Pitts said.

Platinum and palladium users expected Russian supplies would have resumed by now, and have been borrowing the metal to cover their needs, but world inventories have been drawn down in the absence of Russian exports.
"To paraphrase the movie 'Jerry Maguire', its a case of 'show me the metal'," one NYMEX floor trader said said.
"And it's no good blaming hedge funds who have accumulated a stockpile of palladium, as platinum has also hit new highs, and the reality is the Russians are learning about capitalism," he said.
Russian officials told Japanese traders Wednesday that Russian PGM exports would resume on June 20, after a suspension since last December.
Analysts now believe Russia is moving from a marketing strategy based on Soviet-style production and export quotas to one based on price and profit maximization.
Russia supplies about 60 percent of the world's palladium and about 20 percent of its platinum.

Meanwhile, COMEX August gold ended up $2.00 an ounce at $345.60, while in the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $343.10/60, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $340.80 and the New York close Wednesday around $341.00/50.

Implied lease rates for gold rose sharply to 1.45 percent for one month Thursday from 0.82 percent Wednesday in activity believed related to a large South African forward sale program in the past 14 days.
COMEX July silver closed up 7.00 cents at $4.77 an ounce.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
